blocks.text: Processing an image in the spatial domain means working directly on the pixel values themselves — no transformation to another mathematical space is required. This makes spatial domain methods intuitive and computationally efficient. This lecture covers two closely related families: intensity transformations (operations on individual pixels) and spatial filtering (operations on each pixel's neighbourhood).
The operator model

All spatial domain processing can be expressed as g(x, y) = T[ f(x, y) ], where f(x, y) is the input image, g(x, y) is the output image, and T is an operator defined over a neighbourhood around point (x, y).

blocks.title: Two special cases
blocks.text: When the neighbourhood is just one pixel, T reduces to s = T(r) — this is an intensity transformation. When the neighbourhood is larger than one pixel, T looks at surrounding pixels — this is spatial filtering.

blocks.text: Gamma (power-law) transformation
The gamma transformation maps input intensity r to output intensity s using a power function: s = c · r^γ, where c is a positive constant (usually 1) and γ (gamma) controls the shape of the curve.

blocks.caption: Effect of gamma value
rows: Expands dark tones — brightens the image
Compresses dark tones — darkens the image

blocks.title: Why gamma matters
blocks.text: Camera sensors and display monitors do not respond to light linearly. Gamma correction compensates for this non-linearity. When you adjust brightness in a photo editor, you are almost always applying a gamma transformation.
Logarithmic transformation

The logarithm compresses a very wide range of input values into a narrower output range using the formula g = c · log(1 + f). It is especially useful when the image has a few very bright pixels that would otherwise dominate the display.

blocks.title: Classic use case
blocks.text: The magnitude spectrum of a Fourier transform has values ranging over many orders of magnitude. Without log compression, the high-frequency components are invisible. Applying the log transform makes the full spectrum visible.
Contrast stretching

Contrast stretching takes a narrow band of input intensities and maps it to a wider output range. If an image uses only levels 80–120 out of a possible 0–255, contrast stretching redistributes those values across the full 0–255 range, making the image appear much higher in contrast.

blocks.question: Which gamma value brightens an image by expanding dark tones?
blocks.explanation: When γ < 1, the power-law curve bends upward — dark input values map to brighter outputs, expanding the shadow region of the tonal range.

blocks.text: An image histogram is a bar chart that counts how many pixels in the image have each possible intensity value. For an 8-bit grayscale image, there are 256 possible values (0–255), so the histogram has 256 bars. Formally: h(r_k) = n_k, where r_k is intensity level k and n_k is the number of pixels with that intensity.

blocks.caption: Reading a histogram
rows: High contrast — full dynamic range used

blocks.title: Diagnostics first
blocks.text: The histogram is a powerful diagnostic tool. Before applying any enhancement, inspect the histogram to understand what problem you are solving.
Histogram equalization

Histogram equalization redistributes the pixel intensities so the histogram becomes approximately flat (uniform). The result is a full-contrast image that uses the entire available intensity range. The transformation uses the cumulative distribution function (CDF): s_k = (L - 1) · Σ p(r_j) for j = 0 to k, where p(r_j) = n_j / N is the probability of intensity r_j.

blocks.title: When to use histogram equalization
blocks.text: Works best on images with a narrow intensity distribution (low contrast) where the histogram is bunched up toward one end. Does not work well on images that are already high-contrast or that have multimodal histograms (multiple distinct peaks).
CLAHE — Contrast-Limited Adaptive Histogram Equalization

Global histogram equalization applies the same transformation to every pixel. CLAHE solves the problem of uneven lighting by: (1) dividing the image into small rectangular tiles, (2) performing histogram equalization independently on each tile, (3) recombining tiles using bilinear interpolation to avoid sharp boundaries, and (4) applying a clip limit to prevent over-amplification of noise.

blocks.question: Why is CLAHE preferred over global histogram equalization for unevenly lit images?
options: CLAHE uses a log transform instead of a CDF
CLAHE applies equalization to local tiles independently, handling different lighting across regions
CLAHE converts the image to RGB before processing
CLAHE uses the median instead of the mean for redistribution
blocks.explanation: Global equalization uses a single CDF for the whole image. CLAHE computes a separate equalization for each tile, so regions with different exposure levels are handled appropriately.

blocks.text: Spatial filtering goes beyond single-pixel transformations. The output at each pixel is computed from the values of the pixel and its neighbours. This makes it possible to detect patterns, blur detail, sharpen edges, and remove noise — operations that are fundamentally relational between neighbouring pixels.
Linear spatial filtering

In linear spatial filtering, the output is a weighted sum of neighbourhood pixel values: g(x, y) = Σ Σ w(s, t) · f(x+s, y+t), where w(s, t) are the kernel coefficients. This is called correlation when the kernel slides as-is, and convolution when the kernel is rotated 180° first. For symmetric kernels (like a Gaussian), both produce identical results.

blocks.text: Nonlinear spatial filtering — the median filter

Nonlinear spatial filtering uses the same sliding-window mechanics but replaces the weighted sum with a nonlinear operation — typically sorting or ranking the neighbourhood values. The median filter replaces each pixel with the median (middle value) of its neighbourhood.

steps.title: Sort
steps.text: Sort the list from lowest to highest value

steps.title: Write
steps.text: Write that value as the output pixel and move the window

blocks.title: Why the median beats the mean for impulse noise
blocks.text: A single outlier pixel (e.g., a salt or pepper spike) cannot move the median much, but it can dramatically shift the mean. The median filter is the standard tool for removing salt-and-pepper noise.

blocks.question: You have an image corrupted by salt-and-pepper noise. Which filter should you use?
blocks.explanation: The median filter is robust to outliers. A single extreme pixel (salt or pepper) cannot shift the median significantly, while averaging or Gaussian filters would spread the spike into surrounding pixels.

blocks.caption: Method selection guide
rows: Improve local contrast in uneven lighting

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.text: If you need to preserve edges while reducing noise, prefer the median filter over any linear filter. Linear filters blur edges because they average across boundaries.

cards.front: What does γ < 1 do to an image?
cards.back: Expands dark tones — the image becomes brighter overall.

cards.front: When should you use CLAHE instead of global histogram equalization?
cards.back: When illumination varies across the image — CLAHE processes each local tile independently.

cards.front: What is the key difference between correlation and convolution?
cards.back: Convolution rotates the kernel 180° before sliding. For symmetric kernels the results are identical.

cards.front: Why does the median filter preserve edges better than averaging?
cards.back: The median picks an actual pixel value from the neighbourhood — it cannot create new blended values that smear across an edge.
